question: What is the difference between style and substance in fly casting?
answer: Style refers to the individual characteristics a caster brings to execution — arc, elbow position, wrist involvement, body rotation. Substance is the underlying mechanics that make any cast work regardless of style — rod tip path, loop formation, timing of haul and stop. Style is personal. Substance is universal. Teaching style as if it were substance is the most common error in fly casting instruction.

question: What is casting intent in fly fishing?
answer: Intent means knowing exactly what you want the line and fly to do before you make the cast — then selecting the style and applying the mechanics to produce that specific result. A presentation cast into a headwind requires different intent than a reach cast across a seam. When intent is clear, style naturally organizes itself in service of the goal.

question: Why do different expert fly casters look so different?
answer: Expert casters can look very different from each other because style — the individual expression of mechanics — varies from person to person. What they share is substance: correct rod tip path, proper loop formation, and efficient force application. Teaching stylistic traits without understanding the mechanics underneath produces imitation without comprehension.

question: Who developed the style and substance framework for fly casting?
answer: The foundational work on style and substance in fly casting was conducted by Al Kyte and Gary Moran in California during the 1980s. Their contributions to understanding why casting works — not just what to do — set a standard that Mac Brown has built on throughout his teaching career at the Fly Fishing Guide School.
